topic: The Windmill Problem (Computational Geometry & Convex Hulls)

sections.title: Introduction: The Setting
sections.content: Define the windmill problem: n points in a plane, with a line passing through one point acting as a pivot. The line rotates until it hits another point, then pivots around that new point, continuing indefinitely.
sections.example: Visualize a group of n fireflies (points) in a dark forest. A laser beam (the line) pivots around one firefly until it illuminates another, creating a rhythmic, rotating motion.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Angular Sweeping
sections.content: Explain the concept of angular velocity and the 'sweep' operation. Introduce how we sort points by their polar angle relative to the pivot point to determine the next collision point.
sections.example: Imagine a radar screen scanning clockwise; the moment the radar beam touches a firefly, that becomes the new center of rotation.

sections.title: The Mechanical Logic: State Transitions
sections.content: Explain the step-by-step logic: (1) Identify current pivot P1 and point P2. (2) Calculate angles of all other points relative to P1. (3) Choose the point that requires the smallest clockwise rotation. (4) Update P1 to this new point.
sections.example: A mechanical windmill where the blade is a rigid rod. As it hits a pin (point), the rod's rotation center shifts to that pin, mimicking a 'bouncing' or 'revolving' motion.

sections.title: Core Insight: Periodicity and Convex Hull
sections.content: Discuss the 'Invariance' principle: The line covers every possible pair of points. Prove that the rotation is cyclic and the set of edges visited relates to the rotating calipers algorithm used in convex hulls.
sections.example: An animation showing the laser beam tracing all possible diagonals of the set of points, effectively 'knitting' the entire convex structure of the shape.

sections.title: Conclusion & Application
sections.content: Summarize how this illustrates geometric stability and algorithmic complexity. Connect it to real-world applications like path planning and collision detection.
sections.example: Using the windmill logic to design a robot arm that moves between targets in a crowded room without crossing pre-set boundaries.
